newsitem.title: CHINA: FOCUS-Steady growth, low inflation seen for China.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Steady growth, low inflation seen for China.

text.p: China's economy is seen holding steady in the first half of 1997 but low inflation is expected to spur growth in the second half to create a strong finish for the full year, economists said on Wednesday.

China has yet to release most of its economic indicators for the first half but economists forecast the data will show gross domestic product (GDP) growth in a tight range around the first quarter level of 9.4 percent.
Estimates by Chinese economists and analysts in Hong Kong ranged from 9.3 to 9.6 percent.
"For quarter two we are looking for continued deceleration in economic growth," said Charles Li, a regional economist for Natwest Markets in Hong Kong.
Li said that based on data already available, GDP for the first six months would be slightly lower than the fairly strong first quarter figure.
"I haven't seen any significant improvement in industrial production, investment or in retail sales," Li said.
Other analysts said growth could be as high as 9.6 percent, above the official target of eight percent for the full year but still below the 9.8 percent in the same period last year.

"The first half was pretty strong," said Joanne Yim, senior economic research manager at Hang Seng Bank in Hong Kong, adding that she expected GDP growth would come in at 10 percent for the full year.

A Chinese government think tank recently said GDP would grow by 10.3 percent this year, surpassing the 9.0 to 9.5 percent estimate of a senior central banker and a target of 8.0 percent set by Premier Li Peng.
Many smaller enterprises had held back output to trim inventories during the first half, said Xu Hongyuan, an economist with the State Information Centre of the State Planning Commission.
While this limited growth in the first six months it also helped keep the lid on inflation, he said.

China's success in holding down once-rampant inflation could lead to stronger growth in the second half if Beijing grew confident enough to ease credit to ailing state-owned companies, other economists said.
"Inflation has been surprisingly low," said a Hong Kong-based analyst who declined to be identified.

"Many state enterprises are in a bad financial position -- they need money and are requesting easy credit," he said, adding that low inflation could make it easier for the central bank to relax credit slightly during the second half.
China's benchmark retail price inflation inched up by just 0.8 percent in June and Beijing has said the figure will come in at less than two percent for the first half of the year.
Economists said they saw retail inflation for all of 1997 at about 3.0 to 4.0 percent, well below the 6.1 percent in 1996 and the 14.8 percent of 1995.
"To help loss-making enterprises it is possible the government will slightly ease credit... and this is why the economy will pick up just a little bit," the Hong Kong economist said.
Speedier growth could also come about as the result of a recent ban by Beijing on the use of bank loans to speculate in the country's fledgling stock markets, Li said.
Twin interest rate cuts last year had failed to spur economic growth because many companies poured funds into the stock market, fuelling a speculative surge that Beijing has since tried to contain.
"They are trying to curb the funds flowing into the stock markets and force them into the real economy," Li said.
